1578039289434472452.a: I'm giving Bottles a try on Ubuntu 22.04. Flatpak based Windows application installer. It is aware of the Windows applications dependencies and downloads them from the various vendors. Bottles creates a new Wine bottle and then preps it with everything the application needs. t.co

1578039292525514753.a: Fusion works decently under WINE 7.xx staging. Lots of stuff that was broken seems to be fixed. WINE 7.13 and above is starting to feel like a regular Windows system. Window layering is the biggest issue and some buggy third party libraries like their webviewer for the A360 pane.

1578039294807138305.a: Why does it take so many tweaks to make Windows apps work under WINE? Windows includes a database of apps/libraries that need features/bugs from old operating systems. We called them compatibility wedges; I forget the Microsoftspeak. WINE has no built-in compatibility database.

1578039296904372225.a: I learned C by porting UNIX software to Windows and vice-versa. Most of that process USED TO involve writing wedges that implement some feature the target operating system is missing: MinGW FTW. Windows does this on the binaries of third party apps since they have no source code.

1578039298888286208.a: tldr; Bottles installer replicates some missing Windows functionality in WINE for enabling app-specific backward compatibility (with older windows versions) as well as a adding the ability to install known-working dependencies from third party vendors. e.g. some apps need DotNet.
